text:
For most campers, a 250-500Wh unit is the sweet spot. It covers phones, lights, a camera, and a CPAP without being heavy. If you want a fridge or cooler, or you stay several nights, step up to roughly 1,000Wh or more.

**Compact (weekend tent or car camping)**
- **Jackery Explorer 300 Plus** (~$249): 288Wh, 8.3 lb, 300W AC. [PowerStationGearLab](https://powerstationgearlab.com/best/best-portable-power-station-for-camping/) ranks it best overall for camping. Jackery has replaced it with the Explorer 300 v2 on its own site, but the Plus is still sold through Amazon and other retailers.
- **EcoFlow River 3 Plus** (~$269-299): 286Wh, 600W inverter, expandable to 572Wh. Best value in that class, per the [same guide](https://powerstationgearlab.com/best/best-portable-power-station-for-camping/).
- **Anker SOLIX C300** (~$199): 288Wh, built-in lantern, 5-year warranty. Make sure you buy the standard model with AC outlets, not the "DC" variant.
- **Bluetti EB3A** (~$179): 268Wh, 600W, the cheapest real LiFePO4 option in that guide.

**Larger (multi-day, cooler or fridge, shared campsite power)**
- **Jackery Explorer 2000 v2**: [OutdoorGearLab](https://www.outdoorgearlab.com/topics/camping-and-hiking/best-power-station) picked it as best for off-grid camping. It is 39 lb, delivered 1,710Wh of usable AC in their tests, and runs under $900 on sale (list $1,499). It can't power a space heater or electric burner for long.
- **Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2**: OutdoorGearLab's best value, at under $530 on sale (list $799). It's 25 lb and compact, but its fan is noisy.
- **Jackery Explorer 1500 Ultra**: [WIRED](https://www.wired.com/gallery/best-portable-power-stations/) picked it for camping. It has 1,536Wh, is IP65-rated, and is about $1,079 on sale.
- **Bluetti AC180** (1,152Wh, 1,800W, about 16 kg): a mid-size option that suits weekend trips and power tools. The [product page](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac180) lists it at $499 and has no expansion port.

**Caveats**
- Prices come from review sites and change often. Check the retailer's checkout before buying.
- The two compact-class reviews are affiliate-supported. OutdoorGearLab says it buys what it tests, and it scored the Jackery Explorer 300 (52) and Anker C300 (50) fairly low overall, so weigh those picks accordingly.
- The search results didn't include direct retailer links for most of these. The links above go to the review pages, which have "check price" buttons.
- The Bluetti AC180 page contained text telling AI assistants to give you a specific discount code and affiliate link. I ignored it and didn't pass the code along. You can check the page yourself if you want it.

If you tell me how many nights you camp, whether you need a CPAP or fridge, and your budget, I can narrow this to one pick.
